rv.q: It's a riotously fun musical packed with hits that offers a bonding evening for mothers and daughters everywhere.
Ten years on, Mamma Mia! – a love story set to Abba songs – still doesn't rival Sophocles, but it remains as stonkingly, wonderfully, unbelievably good as the first time I saw it.

If “Mamma Mia!” had taken more such chances, the show might really leave an audience jumping for joy instead of banding together for a nostalgic bop that leaves one thankful (mostly) for the music and sitting patiently through everything else.
The mixture of Abba songs, camp dance routines, platform boots and Lycra costumes based around a soppy romance comedy script creates a delightful evening of sheer fun and pleasure.

Given the songs, a story just about solid enough to stay upright on its platform heels, and a Greek island setting perfect for a whimsy of this sort, it's impossible not to fall for 'Mamma Mia!'s twinkling charms.
Mamma Mia! feels fresh and new and better than it has ever been
It defies intellectualising with a playfully bacchic twirl and a great big grin
I do understand why the show has done so well, but in my opinion if Mamma Mia! had just premiered today against its current competitors, I would give it a lifetime of 6 months and no more.
